clinicalPearls: Increased urinary oxalate excretion caused by intestinal fat malabsorption, leading to calcium oxalate stones and, when severe, oxalate nephropathy
Typical settings are Crohn's disease, extensive small-bowel resection, chronic pancreatic insufficiency and malabsorptive bariatric surgery such as Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
Malabsorbed fatty acids bind luminal calcium (saponification), leaving free oxalate available for colonic absorption, while unabsorbed bile salts increase colonic permeability to oxalate
Patients often also have a low urine volume, low urinary citrate and low urinary calcium, all compounding the stone risk
It must be distinguished from primary hyperoxaluria, which is a genetic overproduction of oxalate rather than a malabsorptive state
Severe cases can cause tubulointerstitial oxalate deposition (oxalate nephropathy) and progressive renal failure
Management includes a low-oxalate and low-fat diet, oral calcium or calcium citrate taken with meals to bind luminal oxalate, generous fluids and citrate supplementation
Treating the underlying malabsorption and maintaining hydration are central to prevention
reference.pathophysiology: In health, dietary oxalate in the gut lumen binds calcium and is excreted in the stool. When fat is malabsorbed, unabsorbed long-chain fatty acids preferentially bind calcium (saponification), leaving oxalate free and soluble for absorption in the colon; unabsorbed bile acids further increase colonic permeability to oxalate. The excess absorbed oxalate is excreted by the kidney, raising urinary oxalate which, together with the low urine volume and low citrate that commonly accompany diarrhoeal states, drives calcium oxalate supersaturation and stone formation. With a heavy oxalate burden, tubulointerstitial deposition of calcium oxalate can injure the kidney directly.
additionalDifferentials: Dietary hyperoxaluria from excessive oxalate intake
Other causes of chronic tubulointerstitial disease
Distal renal tubular acidosis with stones
additionalInvestigations: 24-hour urine showing raised oxalate with low volume and low citrate
Assessment of the underlying gastrointestinal disorder, including surgical history and malabsorption workup
Stone analysis confirming calcium oxalate composition
Faecal fat or other markers of fat malabsorption where relevant
Renal biopsy where oxalate nephropathy is suspected
redFlags: A rising creatinine suggesting oxalate nephropathy
Rapid stone recurrence with declining renal function
reference.prognosis: With dietary modification, luminal calcium binding, hydration and control of the bowel disease the stone risk can be reduced; heavy persistent hyperoxaluria may cause oxalate nephropathy and progressive chronic kidney disease.
pitfalls: Restricting dietary calcium, which worsens oxalate absorption
Overlooking hyperoxaluria as a cause of renal decline after bariatric surgery
Neglecting hydration and citrate replacement in chronic diarrhoeal states
management: Adopt a low-oxalate, low-fat diet while maintaining dietary calcium to bind luminal oxalate and reduce its absorption
Give oral calcium with meals as an oxalate binder, and consider a bile-acid sequestrant such as cholestyramine where unabsorbed bile salts drive colonic oxalate absorption
Maintain a high fluid intake to raise urine volume and reduce calcium oxalate supersaturation
Correct hypocitraturia with potassium citrate or alkali therapy to inhibit stone formation
Treat the underlying gastrointestinal disorder and fat malabsorption, whether Crohn's disease, pancreatic insufficiency or post-bariatric anatomy
Monitor urinary oxalate, citrate and volume with renal function, and manage stones urologically as needed
Watch for and manage oxalate nephropathy and progressive chronic kidney disease with nephrology input
